name: DNOW Inc.

profile.description: DNOW Inc. is a Houston-based distributor of pipe, valves, fittings, flanges, MRO supplies, artificial lift, pumping, process and measurement equipment, plus supply-chain and materials-management services, to the upstream, midstream, downstream, utility and industrial markets [4]. Founded in 1862 and spun off from National Oilwell Varco in 2014, the company closed its all-stock acquisition of MRC Global on November 6, 2025, creating the largest energy and industrial PVF distributor in North America [2]. CEO Dave Cherechinsky (since 2020) is leading integration, including stabilizing MRC Global's legacy Oracle ERP and migrating U.S. locations onto DNOW's SAP platform [2]. Q2 2026 revenue was $1.31B (+108% YoY, +10% sequentially), and the company reports Q3 2026 results on November 5, 2026 [1].

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): The defining move of the last five years is the November 2025 all-stock acquisition of MRC Global, which more than doubled revenue (Q2 2026 revenue $1.31B, +108% YoY) and broadened DNOW's mix toward midstream, gas utility and downstream customers [1][2]; this is an M&A-driven scale transformation rather than a new product or business model, so it earns one point. AI Deployment (0/2): Searches of 2026 earnings commentary surfaced no AI-powered customer products or quantified AI savings; management's technology agenda is dominated by the ERP recovery and SAP migration [2]. Market Share (2/2): The combined DNOW/MRC Global is the largest PVF distributor serving North American energy and industrial markets, with a scale advantage in purchasing and inventory breadth that smaller distributors lack [2][4]. Product Pipeline (0/2): Management is targeting data-center and midstream growth, but there are no named next-generation offerings with launch dates or revenue visibility [2]. R&D Intensity (0/1): DNOW reports zero R&D expense in its income statement [5].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): DNOW describes itself as a 'premier energy and industrial solutions provider', a positioning statement that is interchangeable with any industrial distributor and does not articulate a purpose beyond serving customers [2]. Community Impact (1/2): The 2024 Sustainability Report ('Cultivating Sustainable Value', published August 2025 under SASB/TCFD) describes employee community engagement and a 24% YoY drop in total recordable incident rate, but discloses no foundation or dollar-quantified community investment, so it earns general credit only [3]. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention or tenure data was found, and analysts flagged talent retention and sales-team alignment as integration risks after the MRC merger [2]. Insider Buying (0/2): FMP insider data shows zero open-market purchases in 2025-2026 and four insider sales in Q3 2026 (726K shares disposed vs. 405K acquired, mostly grants) [6].

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on growth metrics. D/E of 30.9% scores 1.0 and the forward P/E of 19.2x scores 1.0 (yfinance) [4]. Revenue growth of 108.1% YoY (most recent quarter, inflated by the MRC Global acquisition) scores 1.0, and the 5-year revenue CAGR of 11.7% (FY2020 $1.62B to FY2025 $2.82B, derived from FMP annual statements) scores 1.0 at 2x weight [5]. ROE of -11.6% (2x weight) and profit margin of -4.6% both score 0.0, reflecting a TTM net loss driven by acquisition, integration and ERP-related charges (FY2025 net loss of $89M versus $81M profit in FY2024) [5]. Forward PEG is excluded (null): the provider's forward PEG of 0.25 is computed off a negative earnings base and is not meaningful. Weighted sum 5.00 / 8 = 6.25, rounded to 6. Liquidity floor cleared at ~$38.6M average daily dollar volume.

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): DNOW's revenue comes from physically stocking and delivering pipe, valves, fittings, pumps and MRO supplies from a network of branches to energy and industrial job sites, work AI cannot substitute [4]. No analyst coverage found flags AI as a risk, and AI-driven data-center construction is something management is targeting as a new demand source [2]. The residual exposure is competitive rather than substitutive: larger distributors with stronger digital and data platforms could use AI pricing and demand forecasting to win share while DNOW is consumed by ERP remediation. AI Opportunity (0/1): DNOW discloses no AI-related revenue, and its data-center push sells conventional PVF and electrical products [2].

infinite_game.summary: Through Sinek's lens, DNOW is a durable but finite player: 160+ years of heritage and a conservative balance sheet keep it in the game, yet its strategic language is about scale, synergies (raised to a ~$30M 2026 run-rate from $17M) and market share rather than a cause people would sacrifice for [2]. The MRC Global merger was bold, but it was a consolidation play, and the ERP stumbles that followed show how much the combined company now depends on execution. Leadership continuity under Cherechinsky gives the organization a stable center, but there is no evidence of a Just Cause or a learning-oriented view of rivals.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (0/3): DNOW's self-description as a 'premier energy and industrial solutions provider' names a market position, not a future state worth sacrificing for [2]. Management communication centers on synergies, EBITDA margins (Q3 guide 5-5.5%) and share recovery, with no articulated purpose beyond supplying customers efficiently [1].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Cherechinsky has led since 2020, and before the merger closed he named a combined leadership team drawing from both companies, while publicly emphasizing 'a culture of service and engagement' centered on employees [2]. Offsetting that, the integration has involved a 'much heavier lift than previously known' on ERP, headcount synergies, and analyst-flagged talent-retention risk, so trust is adequate but not exceptional [2].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): DNOW's competitive framing is about becoming the largest PVF distributor through acquisition and 'market-share recovery initiatives' [1]. No management commentary was found acknowledging what rivals such as Wesco or Ferguson do better or using them as a benchmark for self-improvement.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): DNOW has evolved from an upstream-heavy oilfield distributor into a broader midstream, downstream, utility and industrial supplier, a shift the MRC merger accelerated, and it is now targeting data centers [2]. The core model of distributing physical industrial products is unchanged, so this is incremental adaptation rather than reinvention.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Merging with MRC Global in an all-stock deal, doubling the company's size and taking on a troubled legacy ERP, was a high-risk long-term bet that cost near-term profitability (FY2025 net loss of $89M) [2][5]. However, it was a financially motivated consolidation rather than a principled sacrifice in service of a cause, so it earns partial credit.

investment_thesis: DNOW at $15.80 offers an earnings-recovery story built on scale. The MRC Global combination produced Q2 2026 revenue of $1.31B (+108% YoY, +10% sequentially), management raised its 2026 outlook, and Q3 guidance calls for low-to-mid single-digit sequential growth with EBITDA margins of 5-5.5% [1]. The annualized cost-synergy run rate expected by year-end 2026 was raised to ~$30M from an original $17M target [2]. The balance sheet is conservative (D/E 30.9%, current ratio 2.1x), TTM free cash flow yield is ~4.8%, and the stock trades at 19.2x forward earnings and ~0.7x sales [4][5]. Data-center and midstream build-outs offer new demand on top of the core energy business, and the Inspire Impact Score of 41 (ALIGNED, no negative attributions) supports faith-aligned ownership.
thesis_continued: The bear case is execution and cyclicality. The business is unprofitable on a GAAP basis (TTM profit margin -4.6%, ROE -11.6%) because of merger charges, and management called MRC Global's ERP problems 'a much heavier lift than previously known'; half of U.S. revenue runs on the legacy platform being migrated to SAP [2][5]. Organic momentum is thin: management said Q2 revenue was roughly flat excluding a large non-recurring Q1 project and share-recovery efforts [1]. Revenue remains tied to oil and gas capital spending, which fell sharply in 2015-2016 and 2020 (FY2020 net loss of $427M) [5]. The Q3 report on November 5, 2026 is a near-term test of the margin guide [1].
key_catalysts: Q3 2026 results on November 5, 2026 — delivering the guided 5-5.5% EBITDA margin and sequential growth would confirm that MRC integration is moving from remediation to recovery [1]
Synergy delivery — the year-end 2026 annualized cost-synergy run rate was raised to ~$30M from $17M; further upside as U.S. MRC locations finish migrating to SAP [2]
New end markets — data-center construction and midstream gas infrastructure are being pursued as growth vectors beyond traditional upstream oil and gas [2]
key_risks: ERP and integration execution — legacy MRC Global Oracle instability has already disrupted operations and share; a botched SAP migration could cost customers and delay synergies [2]
Energy capex cyclicality — DNOW lost $427M in FY2020 when oil and gas spending collapsed, and a renewed downturn in drilling or midstream budgets would hit volumes directly [5]
Weak organic growth — excluding acquisition effects and a non-recurring Q1 project, Q2 revenue was roughly flat, so the 108% YoY headline overstates underlying demand [1]
